newsitem.title: USA: Fortuna Alliance to pay refunds under settlement.
newsitem.headline: Fortuna Alliance to pay refunds under settlement.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said on Monday that Fortuna Alliance LLC, a firm accused of conducting an Internet pyramid scheme, entered a settlement to refund about $5 million to its members.

The FTC said it charged in a civil complaint that Fortuna and four officers marketed the pyramid scheme through the Internet and printed promotional materials. Thousands of members paid between $250 and $1,750 to join after Fortuna claimed members would get $5,000 a month, the FTC said.
Fortuna Alliance could not immediately be reached for comment.

A statement issued by Fortuna Alliance on June 2, 1996, described it as a "profit sharing cooperative" based in Bellingham, Wash. In that statement, Fortuna had said it would fight a temporary restraining order obtained by the FTC.

Under the settlement of the charges, Fortuna will set aside $2.8 million to fund a consumer redress program, the FTC said. An earlier federal court ruling directed the return of $2 million and an additional $350,000 remains frozen in U.S. banks, FTC said.
The settlement is not an admission of guilt by Fortuna Alliance, the FTC said.
The FTC said the U.S. Department of Justice's Office of Foreign Litigation obtained a court order in Antigua freezing Fortuna funds that have been transferred to an offshore bank there.
The FTC sought a permanent injunction against Fortuna, repatriation of funds transferred offshore and redress for consumers, the agency said.

An FTC spokeswoman named three individuals that were part of Fortuna -- Augustine Delgado, Libby Gustine Welch and Donald Grant -- but the spokeswoman did not have the name of the fourth individual in the settlement.
An FTC spokeswoman later said Monique Delgado was the fourth individual involved in the settlement.
About 30,000 customers were involved with Fortuna Alliance, the spokeswoman said.
